title: Making a leather drawstring pouch
subtitle: Cut and hand-sew a small leather bag with a punch-cord drawstring closure from vegetable-tanned hide
excerpt: How to make a small leather drawstring pouch from vegetable-tanned leather. Covers marking and cutting the panel, punching the stitching holes, hand-sewing the side seam with a saddle stitch, punching the drawstring holes, and threading the cord.
sourceNotes: Traditional leather craft practice. Period saddlery and harness manuals (pre-1928 public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: Leather tanned using plant-derived tannins (oak bark, chestnut, mimosa). Firmer and stiffer than chrome-tanned leather but takes tooling and burnishing well and develops a rich patina with age. The default material for hand-stitched leatherwork. Sold in cuts, full hides, or shoulders. For a small pouch, a 1.5 to 2.5 mm thickness is suitable.

The standard hand-stitching technique for leather. Two needles are threaded on a single length of waxed thread; each needle passes through the same hole from opposite sides, locking the thread. Saddle stitch is stronger than machine stitching because each stitch locks independently: if one stitch breaks, the rest do not unravel.

content.text: to make a drawstring pouch. The construction is a single rectangle of leather folded in half and stitched up both short sides, with a row of holes along the top fold for the drawstring cord. No glue is needed for a simple pouch.
Mark and cut the leather panel

For a small pouch about 100 x 120 mm finished, cut a piece of 2 mm vegetable-tanned leather 120 mm wide x 260 mm long (the 260 mm gives two 120 mm panels plus 20 mm for the fold and drawstring channel). Use the utility knife against a metal ruler on a cutting board. Cut on the grain side (smooth side) for a clean cut. Mark a fold line at 130 mm from one end.
Mark and punch the stitch holes

Mark the stitch line 4 mm in from both long edges of the panel using a stitching pricking iron or a wing divider. Use a pricking iron to punch holes at 4 to 5 mm intervals along both stitch lines. Punch through a single layer of leather on a wooden block. Mark the drawstring holes: a single row of holes 6 to 8 mm in diameter, spaced 20 mm apart, centred on a line 10 mm down from the fold edge on both halves of the panel when folded.
Fold and saddle stitch the side seams

Fold the leather panel in half at the fold line, grain side out. Clamp the two layers together with bulldog clips. Thread a length of waxed thread (about 4 times the seam length) onto two blunt harness needles, one at each end. Starting at the bottom corner, push both needles through the first hole from opposite sides simultaneously, pull the thread through to equal length on each side. Pass the right needle through the second hole; pull through; pass the left needle through the same hole in the opposite direction; pull tight. This locks each stitch. Work all the way up the seam. Repeat for the other side seam. Finish each seam by backstitching through the last two holes twice, then cutting the thread flush.

Thread a length of 3 mm round leather cord, waxed cotton, or paracord through the drawstring holes: in through the first hole from the front, through all holes in sequence, and out through the last hole. Tie a knot at each end of the cord to prevent it pulling through the end holes. Pull both ends to close the pouch.

attrs.symptom: Stitch holes tear through the leather
attrs.cause: Stitch line placed too close to the edge, or the leather is thin and the hole spacing is too coarse.
attrs.fix: Keep the stitch line at least 4 mm from the cut edge. On thin leather (under 1.5 mm) reduce the hole spacing to 3 mm to prevent tearing between holes.

attrs.symptom: Thread tension uneven across the seam
attrs.cause: One needle was pulled more firmly than the other on each stitch.
attrs.fix: Pull both needles simultaneously and by the same distance on each stitch. Consistent tension is the main saddle-stitch skill; it comes with practice.
